scope: Direct Blaschka/Harvard correspondence reconstructing E. A. Snow as the durable Boston receiving-side intermediary through whom papers, freight/express accounts, customs inspection, inspector carriage, importation expenses and onward museum delivery were coordinated. The register separates physical movement from later financial settlement and tracks the consequences when an address/actor retained in the route ceased to function.
methodological_guard: Do not infer Snow's first name, corporate identity, successor or exact legal status from initials alone. Public-web searches in this pass did not securely identify him in a Boston business directory. The primary archive itself securely supplies the 1893 address and later role descriptions. OCR-corrupt freight wording in BLA-D00140 must be checked against the manuscript image before quotation.

actions: incoming boxes are shipped as before by Ehrhorn, Emden & Mayer and consigned to E. A. Snow
Goodale tells Harvard's Treasurer that Snow was formerly a Custom-house Broker on State Street but is no longer in business
Harvard must 'hunt Snow up and arrange with him'

events.research_value: A routinized address/actor outlives the actor's active business. Transport infrastructure can fail because procedural memory is embedded in paperwork that has become obsolete.

actions: Rudolf instructs R.B. 1–4 to travel Bremen → New York → in bond to Boston, care of E. A. Snow, Customhouse broker and forwarding agent
the Bremen agents later become anxious because the Boston agent E. A. Snow 'does no more exist'
the American Line is asked to provide another agent
Rudolf attributes the delay probably to this failure
events.research_value: The named intermediary had become part of the route itself. His disappearance generated delay, showing path dependence created by institutional memory rather than physical geography alone.

analytical_observations: Snow should not be reduced to 'customs broker'. Across the surviving correspondence he acts at the junction of papers, forwarding, freight and express billing, customs inspection, inspector carriage, commission and museum delivery.
Physical arrival and financial/administrative closure have different clocks. Bills can arrive later and can carry omitted costs from an earlier encounter.
Invoices are evidentially valuable because they can reassemble route segments that correspondence treats separately. They are retrospective maps in accounting form.
The repeated use of Snow from 1892 onward shows durable receiver-side procedural memory; 1906 and 1923 show the fragility of that memory when the individual/firma disappears.

comparison_guard.sound_steamer: The March 1893 bill directly names freight by 'the Ocean and the Sound Steamers' for that shipment. It must not be projected backward onto U.B. 346–350 in 1892 until the 1892 bill, manifest or equivalent route document is found.
comparison_guard.wales_carriage: The September 1893 bill includes a carriage charge from Col. Wales's previous visit that Snow had omitted. The exact earlier inspection event to which the residual charge belongs must be source-checked rather than assumed.
